```markdown
## Study Area and Sampling Strategy

The Steamboat Hot Springs hydrothermal system exhibits spatially heterogeneous surface expressions including springs, fumaroles, creeks, and mixed outflow zones. Sampling locations were selected to capture geochemical gradients along inferred shallow subsurface flow paths, with particular emphasis on transitions from high-temperature fumarolic or spring discharge to downstream mixing zones and surface waters. Site selection was informed by prior studies (e.g., Sorey and Spielman) and updated field reconnaissance following recent changes in hydrothermal surface manifestations.

Sampling locations were treated as persistent spatial entities, while individual samples and measurements were associated with discrete sampling events representing specific field campaigns. This design enables consistent resampling of the same features through time while preserving temporal resolution and campaign-specific metadata.

## Relational Database Design

A relational SQLite database was developed to manage field, laboratory, and legacy geochemical data in a reproducible and extensible framework. The database schema separates spatial entities (Locations), temporal context (Sampling_Events), physical samples (Samples), and analytical observations (Field_Measurements and Lab_Analyses). This normalization prevents data duplication, enforces referential integrity, and allows independent updates to locations, sampling campaigns, and analytical results.

Legacy water-quality data from the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP) were ingested through a dedicated staging table to preserve original structure and provenance prior to controlled mapping into the core schema. Field and laboratory data collected as part of this study were ingested separately using structured spreadsheets and validation routines to ensure consistency and traceability.

## Data Ingestion and Validation

Field data were recorded using standardized spreadsheet templates corresponding to individual database tables. These templates serve as temporary human interfaces and are validated prior to database insertion using automated checks for required fields, allowable values, and foreign key consistency. Laboratory analytical results were normalized from wide-format laboratory reports into a standardized long format, allowing an arbitrary number of analytes, including major ions, trace elements, and isotopes.

All data ingestion steps are scripted and deterministic. Raw input files are not modified during ingestion, and all transformations are explicitly encoded in version-controlled R scripts.


## Quality Control

Automated quality control (QC) checks were applied after data ingestion and prior to geochemical modeling. These checks include validation of field measurement ranges (e.g., pH, temperature, conductivity), detection of missing critical parameters, verification of major ion completeness, and identification of negative or invalid laboratory concentrations.

Consistency between field and laboratory alkalinity measurements was evaluated by comparing paired observations and flagging discrepancies exceeding 15 percent. Charge balance was calculated for each sample using major ion concentrations, and samples exceeding ±5 percent imbalance were flagged. All QC results were recorded in persistent summary tables and exported as user-readable reports to facilitate troubleshooting and documentation.

## Geochemical Modeling Workflow

A derived PHREEQC_Solutions table was generated programmatically from validated field and laboratory data. This table consolidates major ion chemistry, pH, and temperature into a PHREEQC-ready format, with one row representing one aqueous solution. Only samples meeting completeness and charge-balance criteria were used for geochemical modeling.

Forward speciation and inverse geochemical models were executed using PHREEQC and PHREESQL, with the SQLite database serving as both input and output. Model results, including inverse reaction coefficients and residuals, were written back to the database to ensure full reproducibility and traceability between input chemistry and modeled processes.
